title: The Rod and the Breastplate: Aaron of the House of Levi, from the Dust of Egypt to the Cave on Mount Hor
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The House of Levi in Egypt

stops.name: Goshen, the birth in the house of Levi
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. No verse gives Aaron's birth year or birthplace. The year is arithmetic from the Seder Olam anchor of 1313 BCE for the Exodus, at which Exodus 7:7 makes Aaron 83; the place is inferred from the settlement of Israel in the eastern Delta, and Goshen is a region, not a site. The rival Ramesside chronology would move the birth some hundred years later.
stops.campa: Amram of the house of Levi takes Jochebed his father's sister to wife. She bears Miriam, then Aaron, then Moses three years after. The line runs back through Kohath and Levi and Jacob and Isaac to Abraham, and it is a line of herdsmen now living under taskmasters in the pasture country of the eastern Delta. Nothing is set down of Aaron's childhood, nothing of what he saw of the decree against the newborn boys. He is simply there, three years the elder, when his brother is drawn out of the water and carried into Pharaoh's house.
sources: Seder Olam Rabbah (traditional chronology, via secondary summary)
suggested_refs: The Wadi Tumilat and the eastern Delta, the region the text calls the land of Goshen

stops.name: Horeb, the mountain of God: the brothers meet
stops.date_confidence: The meeting is attested; the date is placed shortly before the first audience with Pharaoh on the 1313 BCE reckoning. The identification of the mountain of God with Jabal Musa is Byzantine monastic tradition and carries no textual or archaeological warrant.
stops.campa: The LORD speaks to Aaron in Egypt and tells him to go out into the wilderness. Aaron goes. At the mountain of God he meets Moses, come back from forty years in Midian with a rod in his hand, and he kisses him. The commission was given on this mountain before he arrived, and his share in it was settled without him: he speaks readily, and he will be mouth for a man who does not. Two brothers who have not stood together since childhood walk down into Egypt with one errand between them.
stops.quote: GOD became angry with Moses and said, "There is your brother Aaron the Levite. He, I know, speaks readily. Even now he is setting out to meet you, and he will be happy to see you."
stops.quote_source: Exodus 4:14, THE JPS TANAKH: Gender-Sensitive Edition (Revised JPS, 2023), via Sefaria
suggested_refs: Jabal Musa in the southern Sinai, the traditional mountain of God

stops.name: Goshen, the signs before the elders
stops.date_confidence: Attested as an event, undated in the text; placed here immediately before the first audience with Pharaoh, which the narrative makes follow it directly.
stops.campa: Aaron and Moses gather the elders of the children of Israel. Aaron speaks all the words the LORD gave to Moses, and Moses does the signs in the sight of the people: the rod, the hand made leprous and made whole again. The people believe. They hear that the LORD has visited them and looked upon their affliction, and they bow their heads and worship. Aaron's voice does the work his brother cannot do, and it is the first time. Within days the labor of Israel will be doubled and the same elders will turn on both of them.
suggested_refs: The elders of the children of Israel, the first audience Aaron ever addresses

stops.name: Pi-Ramesses, the first demand before Pharaoh
stops.date_confidence: Attested as an event, undated in the text. The 1313 BCE year follows Exodus 7:7 read against the Seder Olam anchor. The court is placed at Pi-Ramesses rather than at Zoan: Tanis is unattested before the 19th Dynasty and became a capital only later, so Psalm 78's field of Zoan is a retrojection.
stops.campa: The two brothers come into the court of the king of Egypt and say: thus says the LORD God of Israel, let my people go, that they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness. Pharaoh answers that he does not know the LORD and will not let Israel go. That same day he orders the straw withheld and the tale of bricks kept whole. Aaron is eighty-three and has lived his whole life in this country under its overseers. He has now stood in its throne room and told its king what to do.
suggested_refs: Qantir, the site of Pi-Ramesses in the eastern Delta

stops.name: Pi-Ramesses, the rod that becomes a serpent
stops.date_confidence: Attested as an event, undated in the text; placed between the first audience and the plague of blood, the order the narrative gives.
stops.campa: Pharaoh demands a wonder. Aaron casts down his rod before Pharaoh and before his servants, and it becomes a serpent. The king calls his wise men and his sorcerers, and the magicians of Egypt do the same with their enchantments; every man casts down his rod and every rod becomes a serpent. Then Aaron's rod swallows their rods. Rashi says it had turned back into a rod first and swallowed them in that state, which is the greater wonder. Pharaoh's heart is hardened and he does not listen to them.
stops.quote: Each cast down his rod, and they turned into serpents. But Aaron's rod swallowed their rods.
stops.quote_source: Exodus 7:12, THE JPS TANAKH: Gender-Sensitive Edition (Revised JPS, 2023), via Sefaria
sources: Rashi on Exodus 7:9 and 7:12, trans. Rosenbaum and Silbermann, via Sefaria
Shabbat 97a and Exodus Rabbah 9:7, cited by Rashi
suggested_refs: The rod of Aaron, which will reappear before the Testimony forty years later

stops.name: The Nile, the water turned to blood
stops.date_confidence: Attested as an event, undated in the text. Coordinates are a Delta reach of the river, not a located site.
stops.campa: In the morning Pharaoh goes down to the water. Aaron lifts the rod and strikes the river in the sight of the king and his servants, and all the water in it is turned to blood. The fish die, the river stinks, the Egyptians cannot drink of it and dig round about for water. Seven days the plague holds. Moses does not strike this water himself: the river carried him in a basket of bulrushes when he was three months old, and a man does not smite what sheltered him. The elder brother lifts the rod instead.
stops.quote: Because the river had protected Moses when he was cast into it, therefore it was not smitten by him neither at the plague of blood nor at that of frogs, but it was smitten by Aaron.
stops.quote_source: Rashi on Exodus 7:19, trans. M. Rosenbaum and A. M. Silbermann, via Sefaria
suggested_refs: Exodus Rabbah 9:10, the source of the reasoning from the river's debt

stops.name: The canals of Egypt, the frogs
stops.date_confidence: Attested as an event, undated in the text. The chapter and verse differ by system: Hebrew numbering puts Aaron's act at Exodus 8:1-2, English numbering at 8:5-6.
stops.campa: Aaron stretches out his hand with the rod over the streams, the canals, and the pools, and the frogs come up and cover the land of Egypt. They go into the houses and the bedchambers, into the ovens and the kneading troughs. The magicians bring up frogs as well and cannot take a single one away. Pharaoh calls for Moses and Aaron, asks them to entreat the LORD, and promises to let the people go; when there is respite he hardens his heart again. Again it is Aaron's hand over the water, and for the same reason.
sources: Rashi on Exodus 7:19, extending the same reasoning to the frogs
suggested_refs: The two versification systems of the frog plague, Hebrew 7:26-8:11 against English 8:1-15

stops.name: The dust of Egypt, the lice
stops.date_confidence: Attested as an event, undated in the text.
stops.campa: Aaron stretches out his hand with the rod and smites the dust of the earth, and it becomes lice through all the land, on man and on beast. The magicians try with their enchantments to bring forth lice and they cannot. They come to Pharaoh and say: this is the finger of God. It is the last plague any of them attempts to answer. Aaron's rod has done three of them now, and the men whose whole trade was to match a wonder with a wonder have said out loud, in the king's hearing, that they are finished.
suggested_refs: The magicians of Egypt, who answer three signs and then stop

stops.name: Rameses, the night of the going out
stops.date_confidence: The fifteenth of the first month is the date the text itself fixes for the departure; the year is the Seder Olam anchor and is traditional, not attested.
stops.campa: In the night Pharaoh calls for Moses and Aaron and tells them to rise up and get out from among his people, to take their flocks and their herds and be gone, and to bless him also. The children of Israel journey from Rameses, six hundred thousand men on foot besides children, with the dough unleavened on their shoulders because they are thrust out and cannot tarry. Aaron is eighty-three years old. He has never once been outside Egypt except to walk to a mountain and back to fetch his brother.
suggested_refs: Exodus 12:41, the four hundred and thirty years ended on the selfsame day

segments.name: The Sea and the Bitter Water

stops.name: Succoth, the first encampment
stops.date_confidence: The first station is attested; the identification with Tell el-Maskhuta is a modern proposal, and the same tell is elsewhere proposed as Pithom. Coordinates are the tell's.
stops.campa: The people come out of Rameses and pitch at Succoth, the booths. They bake unleavened cakes of the dough they carried out, because it was not leavened and they had prepared no victual. The LORD goes before them in a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night. Aaron walks in a column of six hundred thousand men and their households. It is the first night of a nation with no country. No law has been given yet, and no priest appointed. The bones of Joseph go with them.
suggested_refs: Tell el-Maskhuta in the Wadi Tumilat, proposed as Succoth and also as Pithom

stops.name: Pi-hahiroth, the sea in front and the chariots behind
stops.date_confidence: The encampment is attested; the site is not. The coordinates follow the traditional anchor at Ayun Musa, one candidate among several, and are marked as reconstruction.
stops.campa: Israel turns and camps before Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, over against Baal-zephon. Pharaoh, told that the people have fled, makes ready his chariot and takes six hundred chosen chariots and all the chariots of Egypt, and overtakes them camped by the sea. The people are sore afraid and cry out, and say to Moses that there were graves enough in Egypt. Aaron, who spoke every word of the demand that brought them here, stands with his brother between the water and the horses and has nothing to say.
suggested_refs: Ayun Musa on the Sinai shore, the traditional anchor for Pi-hahiroth

stops.name: The far shore, the song at the sea
stops.date_confidence: The crossing is attested; its location is among the most disputed points in the whole itinerary, with candidates from the Bitter Lakes to Lake Ballah to the Gulf of Aqaba. The seventh day from the departure is the traditional reckoning.
stops.campa: The sea goes back before Moses' outstretched hand and Israel walks over on dry ground, the waters a wall on the right and on the left. The Egyptians follow in and the sea returns to its strength. On the far shore Moses and the children of Israel sing, and Miriam the prophetess, Aaron's sister, takes a timbrel in her hand, and all the women go out after her with timbrels and with dances. The three children of Amram and Jochebed stand on the same beach with the water behind them and no Egypt on the other side.
suggested_refs: The Song of the Sea, Exodus 15, and Miriam's antiphon at its close

stops.name: Marah, the bitter water made sweet
stops.date_confidence: Three days into the wilderness of Shur, per the text. The site is traditionally Ain Hawarah, which has no authoritative published coordinate; the position given is fixed by the itinerary order, since Marah must lie north of Wadi Gharandel, the candidate for the next station.
stops.campa: Three days into the wilderness of Shur they find no water. They come to Marah and cannot drink of its water, for it is bitter, and the people murmur against Moses and ask what they shall drink. The LORD shows him a tree; he casts it into the waters and the waters are made sweet. There the LORD makes for them a statute and an ordinance, and proves them, and says: if you will diligently hearken, I will put none of these diseases upon you, for I am the LORD that heals you.
suggested_refs: Ain Hawarah on the coastal route, the traditional Marah

stops.name: Elim, twelve springs and seventy palms
stops.date_confidence: The station is attested; the identification with Wadi Gharandel is traditional and contested. Har-El argued in 1968 for Uyun Musa on the strength of twelve springs and date palms recorded there in 1907; Hoffmeier objects that Uyun Musa lies only some twelve kilometres from the previous station. Not adjudicated here.
stops.campa: They come to Elim, where there are twelve wells of water and threescore and ten palm trees, and they camp there by the waters. Twelve springs for twelve tribes, seventy palms for the seventy souls of the house of Jacob that went down into Egypt. It is the only station on the road where the text records nothing happening at all: no thirst, no murmuring, no sign, no judgment. They rest. Aaron is eighty-three years old and the priesthood has not yet been mentioned to him.
suggested_refs: Wadi Gharandel and Uyun Musa, the two rival candidates for Elim

stops.name: The wilderness of Sin, the bread from heaven
stops.date_confidence: The fifteenth day of the second month is given by the text. The wilderness of Sin has no secure identification whatsoever; the coordinates are a point on the presumed route and should be read as a placeholder, not a location.
stops.campa: On the fifteenth day of the second month the whole congregation murmurs against Moses and Aaron and says they should have died in Egypt by the fleshpots, where they ate bread to the full. Aaron speaks to the whole assembly of the children of Israel, telling them to come near before the LORD, for he has heard their murmurings. They look toward the wilderness and the glory of the LORD appears in the cloud. At evening the quails come up and cover the camp; in the morning the dew lifts and the small round thing lies on the ground.
suggested_refs: The omer of manna Aaron will later lay up before the Testimony, Exodus 16:33-34

stops.name: Rephidim, the hands held up until sunset
stops.date_confidence: The battle is attested; the identification of Rephidim with the Feiran oasis is one of several traditional proposals and is not secure. The date is placed in the third month, before the arrival at Sinai.
stops.campa: Amalek comes and fights with Israel at Rephidim. Joshua chooses men and goes out; Moses climbs the hill with the rod of God in his hand, and Aaron and Hur go up with him. When Moses holds up his hand Israel prevails, and when he lets it down Amalek prevails. His hands grow heavy. They take a stone and put it under him, and Aaron on the one side and Hur on the other stay up his hands, and his hands are steady until the going down of the sun. Aaron's work here is to hold up an arm that is not his.
suggested_refs: Wadi Feiran, called by Wikipedia only one of the alleged sites of Rephidim

segments.name: Sinai, the Vision and the Calf

stops.name: Mount Sinai, the elders see the God of Israel
stops.date_confidence: The covenant meal is attested; the day is placed in the third month, after the giving of the words and the ordinances. The identification of Sinai with Jabal Musa is Byzantine monastic tradition.
stops.campa: Moses goes up, and Aaron with him, and Nadab and Abihu his sons, and seventy of the elders of Israel. They see the God of Israel, and there is under his feet as it were a paved work of sapphire stone, like the very heaven for clearness. Upon the nobles of the children of Israel he lays not his hand, and they behold God, and eat and drink. Aaron stands in the highest sight the text ever grants to anyone but his brother, with his two eldest sons beside him. Both will be dead within the year.
suggested_refs: The paved work of sapphire stone under the feet of the God of Israel

stops.name: The foot of the mountain, left in charge of the camp
stops.date_confidence: Attested. The camp is placed at Er-Raha, the plain below Jabal Musa, on the same monastic identification that fixes the mountain.
stops.campa: Moses says to the elders: tarry here for us until we come again to you, and behold, Aaron and Hur are with you; if any man have any matters to do, let him come to them. Then Moses goes up into the mount, and the cloud covers it six days, and the glory of the LORD abides on it like devouring fire in the sight of the children of Israel. Moses goes into the cloud and is in the mount forty days and forty nights. Aaron is left holding a nation of six hundred thousand at the foot of a burning mountain.
suggested_refs: The plain of Er-Raha below Jabal Musa, the traditional site of the camp

stops.name: Er-Raha, the calf out of the fire
stops.date_confidence: Attested as an event, undated in the text; placed at the end of the forty days, on the traditional reckoning that puts Moses' descent on the seventeenth of the fourth month.
stops.campa: The people see that Moses delays coming down and gather themselves together to Aaron. Make us gods, they say, to go before us, for as for this Moses we know not what is become of him. Aaron tells them to break off the golden earrings in the ears of their wives and their sons and their daughters and bring them to him. They break them off and bring them, and he receives the gold at their hand and fashions it with a graving tool, and there comes out a molten calf. The people say: these are thy gods, O Israel.
stops.quote: When the people saw that Moses was so long in coming down from the mountain, the people gathered against Aaron and said to him, "Come, make us a god who shall go before us, for we do not know what has happened to Moses ..."
stops.quote_source: Exodus 32:1, THE JPS TANAKH: Gender-Sensitive Edition (Revised JPS, 2023), via Sefaria; the closing clause of the verse is elided
sources: Rashi on Exodus 32:4, citing Midrash Tanchuma, via Sefaria
suggested_refs: Rashi's reading that magicians of the mixed multitude worked the calf out of the melted gold

stops.name: Er-Raha, the altar and the feast set for tomorrow
stops.date_confidence: Attested as an event, undated in the text; the day before Moses' descent on the traditional reckoning.
stops.campa: Aaron sees the calf and builds an altar before it with his own hands, and makes proclamation: tomorrow is a feast to the LORD. Not today. Rashi reads every part of it as delay: Aaron builds the altar himself, slowly, rather than let the people build it, and sets the feast for the morrow hoping Moses will come down before anyone worships. In his heart, Rashi says, his intent was toward Heaven. The people rise up early the next morning, offer burnt offerings, and sit down to eat and to drink, and rise up to play.
stops.quote: HE BUILDED AN ALTAR to put them off ... to-morrow, not to-day, for he hoped that Moses might return before they would worship it.
stops.quote_source: Rashi on Exodus 32:5, trans. M. Rosenbaum and A. M. Silbermann, via Sefaria
suggested_refs: Rashi on Exodus 32:5, the reading of the delayed feast as a stalling tactic

stops.name: Er-Raha, I did not know that this calf would come out
stops.date_confidence: Attested as an event, undated in the text; the seventeenth of the fourth month is the traditional date of the descent and the breaking of the tablets.
stops.campa: Moses comes down, sees the calf and the dancing, casts the tables out of his hands and breaks them beneath the mount, burns the calf, grinds it to powder, strews it on the water and makes the children of Israel drink. Then he turns to his brother: what did this people unto thee, that thou hast brought so great a sin upon them? Aaron answers that he asked only who had gold, that they gave it, that he cast it into the fire. And there came out this calf. The LORD was angry enough with Aaron to destroy him, and Moses prayed for Aaron also at that time.
stops.quote: AND I CAST IT INTO THE FIRE, and I did not know that this (i. e. this living) calf would come out ... BUT IT DID COME OUT.
stops.quote_source: Rashi on Exodus 32:24, trans. M. Rosenbaum and A. M. Silbermann, via Sefaria
suggested_refs: Deuteronomy 9:20, where Moses records the prayer that saved his brother's life

stops.name: Er-Raha, the garments for glory and for beauty
stops.date_confidence: The pattern is given at Exodus 28 and the making reported at Exodus 39, neither dated; placed here before the ordination, which the traditional reckoning puts in the last week of Adar.
stops.campa: Bezalel and the skilled workers finish the garments and bring them to Moses: the breastplate of judgment with four rows of stones, one for each tribe, and the Urim and the Thummim in it; the ephod of gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twined linen; the robe with pomegranates and golden bells around its hem; the tunic, the mitre, the embroidered girdle, and the plate of pure gold engraved Holiness to the LORD. They are made for Aaron, for glory and for beauty, and the man who wore an Egyptian herdsman's cloth is to put them on.
suggested_refs: The Urim and the Thummim carried in the breastplate of judgment

stops.name: The Tent of Meeting, seven days of ordination
stops.date_confidence: The seven days of the milu'im are attested at Leviticus 8; the traditional reckoning places them on the twenty-third to twenty-ninth of Adar, immediately before the erection of the Tabernacle on the first of Nisan in the second year.
stops.campa: Moses gathers the whole congregation to the door of the Tent of Meeting. He washes Aaron and his sons with water, puts the tunic on him and girds him with the sash, clothes him with the robe and the ephod, sets the breastplate on him with the Urim and the Thummim, puts the mitre on his head and the golden plate upon it. He pours the anointing oil on Aaron's head. For seven days they do not go out from the door of the Tent, and the blood of the ram of consecration is put on the tip of Aaron's right ear, his right thumb, and his right great toe.
suggested_refs: The ram of consecration and the seven days of the milu'im

stops.name: The Tabernacle, the eighth day and the fire
stops.date_confidence: The eighth day of Leviticus 9 is counted from the start of the seven days of ordination in Adar, and so falls on the first of Nisan in the second year, the same day the Tabernacle was raised at Exodus 40:17. It is not the eighth of Nisan, as the pool material had it.
stops.campa: On the eighth day Moses calls Aaron and his sons and the elders of Israel. Aaron goes to the altar and offers the calf of the sin offering for himself, then the offerings of the people, and he lifts up his hand toward the people and blesses them and comes down. Moses and Aaron go into the Tent of Meeting, and when they come out and bless the people, the glory of the LORD appears to all the people. Fire comes out from before the LORD and consumes the burnt offering on the altar; the people shout and fall on their faces.
suggested_refs: The priestly blessing Aaron first pronounces here, Numbers 6:22-27

stops.name: The Tabernacle, Nadab and Abihu
stops.date_confidence: The text places the deaths on the same eighth day as the first service, and so on the first of Nisan of the second year on the traditional reckoning.
stops.campa: Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, take each his censer and put fire in it and incense on it, and offer strange fire before the LORD, which he commanded them not. Fire goes out from before the LORD and devours them, and they die before the LORD. Moses tells his brother that this is what the LORD spoke, saying: I will be sanctified in them that come near me. And Aaron holds his peace. He is forbidden to uncover his head or rend his clothes, and forbidden wine when he goes into the Tent. His cousins carry his sons out of the camp by their tunics.
stops.quote_source: Leviticus 10:3, THE JPS TANAKH: Gender-Sensitive Edition (Revised JPS, 2023), via Sefaria; Hebrew vayidom Aharon
suggested_refs: Leviticus 10:6-9, the mourning forbidden and the wine forbidden

stops.name: Er-Raha, the numbering of the host
stops.date_confidence: Numbers 1:1 fixes this on the first day of the second month in the second year after the going out of Egypt. The pool material had dated it a month early, which had wrongly folded it into the ordination cluster.
stops.campa: On the first day of the second month in the second year the LORD speaks to Moses in the Tent of Meeting and tells him to take the sum of all the congregation by their families, by the house of their fathers, every male from twenty years old and upward, all that are able to go forth to war. Moses and Aaron take the men named to them and assemble the whole congregation, and they declare their pedigrees. The tribe of Levi is not numbered among them; Aaron's own house is counted apart, and set over the Tabernacle of the Testimony.
suggested_refs: Numbers 1:47-53, the Levites numbered apart and set over the Tabernacle

segments.name: Paran, the Murmuring and the Revolt

stops.name: Hazeroth, the words against Moses
stops.date_confidence: Attested as an event, undated in the text beyond its position after the departure from Sinai. The identification of Hazeroth with Ain Khadra is traditional.
stops.campa: At Hazeroth, Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses because of the Cushite woman he had married, and say: has the LORD indeed spoken only by Moses, has he not spoken also by us? The LORD hears it and calls the three of them out to the Tent. When the cloud departs, Miriam is leprous, white as snow. Aaron turns to his brother and calls him lord, and begs him not to lay the sin upon them. Both spoke. Only the sister is struck, and the text never says why the priest was not.
stops.quote: Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Cushite woman he had married: "He married a Cushite!"
stops.quote_source: Numbers 12:1, THE JPS TANAKH: Gender-Sensitive Edition (Revised JPS, 2023), via Sefaria
suggested_refs: Ain Khadra in the eastern Sinai, the traditional Hazeroth

stops.name: Kadesh-barnea, the scouts come back
stops.date_confidence: Attested as an event, undated in the text. The identification of Kadesh-barnea with Ein Qudeirat is the standard modern proposal and is reasonably secure by the standards of this itinerary.
stops.campa: From the wilderness of Paran twelve men go up to spy out the land, one ruler of each tribe. They come back after forty days with a cluster of grapes carried on a staff between two of them, and with a report: the land eats up its inhabitants, and the men there are giants. All the congregation lifts up its voice and weeps that night. Moses and Aaron fall on their faces before the whole assembly, and Joshua and Caleb rend their clothes. The congregation talks of stoning them and of choosing a captain to go back to Egypt.
suggested_refs: Ein Qudeirat in the northern Sinai, the standard identification of Kadesh-barnea

stops.name: Kadesh, Korah against the priesthood
stops.date_confidence: The revolt is attested; the text fixes no year for it anywhere within the forty. The date given is a placement within the wilderness period, not a claim.
stops.campa: Korah the son of Izhar, a Levite of Aaron's own clan, with Dathan and Abiram and two hundred and fifty princes of the assembly, rises up against Moses and Aaron. All the congregation are holy, they say; why lift ye up yourselves above the assembly of the LORD? Moses sets the test: let every man take his censer and put incense in it, and Aaron his. In the morning the ground under Dathan and Abiram opens and swallows them and their households, and fire from the LORD consumes the two hundred and fifty men who offered the incense.
suggested_refs: The censers of the two hundred and fifty, beaten into plates for the altar, Numbers 17:1-5

stops.name: Kadesh, the censer between the dead and the living
stops.date_confidence: Attested as an event, undated in the text; it follows Korah's destruction by one day in the narrative.
stops.campa: On the morrow the whole congregation murmurs against Moses and Aaron, saying they have killed the people of the LORD. The plague begins. Moses tells Aaron to take a censer, put fire in it from off the altar and incense on it, and go quickly into the congregation and make atonement. Aaron takes it and runs into the midst of the assembly, and stands between the dead and the living, and the plague is stayed. Fourteen thousand and seven hundred are already dead. This is the one thing Aaron does at a run and on his own feet.
suggested_refs: The censer of incense, the instrument that killed two hundred and fifty men and then stopped a plague

stops.name: Kadesh, the rod that bore almonds
stops.date_confidence: Attested as an event, undated in the text; it follows the censer episode directly in the narrative. Verse numbering differs by system: Numbers 17:16-23 in the Hebrew, 17:1-8 in the English.
stops.campa: Twelve rods are laid up before the Testimony, one for each prince of the fathers' houses, and Aaron's name is written on the rod of Levi. The next day Moses goes into the Tent of the Testimony and the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi has budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded ripe almonds. Rashi asks why almonds and not another fruit, and answers that the almond blossoms faster than any other, and so too the punishment of a man who sets himself against the priesthood comes quickly.
stops.quote: The next day Moses entered the Tent of the Pact, and there the staff of Aaron of the house of Levi had sprouted: it had brought forth sprouts, produced blossoms, and borne almonds.
stops.quote_source: Numbers 17:23, THE JPS TANAKH: Gender-Sensitive Edition (Revised JPS, 2023), via Sefaria
suggested_refs: Rashi's example of swift punishment: the leprosy that broke out on King Uzziah's forehead

stops.name: Kadesh, the death of Miriam
stops.date_confidence: The first month of the fortieth year is given by the text, which does not name the day. The year follows the Seder Olam anchor.
stops.campa: In the first month the children of Israel come again into the desert of Zin and abide in Kadesh. There Miriam dies, and there she is buried. She is the eldest of the three, the one who stood at a distance to see what would be done to the basket in the reeds, the one who sang with the timbrel on the far shore. There is no water for the congregation. Aaron is a hundred and twenty-two years old and has four months left, and he has just buried the sister who watched over both her brothers before either could speak.
suggested_refs: Numbers 20:1, the death of Miriam and the drying of the well that followed her

stops.name: Meribah, the rock struck twice
stops.date_confidence: Attested as an event, undated in the text beyond its position in the first month of the fortieth year.
stops.campa: The people chide with Moses and say: would God that we had died when our brethren died before the LORD. Moses and Aaron go from the assembly to the door of the Tent and fall on their faces. Take the rod, says the LORD, and speak ye unto the rock. Moses lifts his hand and smites the rock twice with the rod, and the water comes out abundantly, and the congregation drinks and their beasts also. Then: because ye believed me not, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel, ye shall not bring this assembly into the land. Both of them.
suggested_refs: Numbers 20:12, the sentence pronounced on Moses and Aaron together

stops.name: Mount Hor, the garments taken off
stops.date_confidence: Numbers 33:38 fixes the first day of the fifth month in the fortieth year after the going out of Egypt; on the traditional reckoning that is the first of Av. The identification of Mount Hor with Jabal Harun above Petra is traditional, held in common by Jewish, Christian, and Muslim veneration.
stops.campa: The congregation journeys from Kadesh and comes to Mount Hor, on the edge of the land of Edom. The LORD tells Moses to take Aaron and Eleazar his son and bring them up the mountain, and to strip Aaron of his garments and put them on Eleazar. They go up in the sight of all the congregation. On the summit Moses takes off the mitre, the breastplate, the ephod, the robe, and puts each one on Eleazar while his father stands there and watches, and Aaron is a man in a plain tunic again for the first time in thirty-nine years.
suggested_refs: Jabal Harun above Petra, venerated as Mount Hor by Jews, Christians, and Muslims alike

stops.name: Mount Hor, the cave and the made bed
stops.date_confidence: The death on the mountain is attested at Numbers 20:28 and dated by Numbers 33:38. The cave, the bed, the lamp, and the sequence of instructions are Rashi's, drawn from midrash, and are tradition rather than text.
stops.campa: Moses leads his brother to a cave in the rock. Inside there is a bed already made and a lamp already burning. Enter the cave, he says, and Aaron enters. Ascend the bed, and he ascends. Stretch out your hands, and he stretches them out. Close your mouth, and he closes it. Close your eyes, and he closes them. So Aaron dies there in the top of the mount, a hundred and twenty-three years old, and Moses, watching him go like that, wishes such a death for himself. Moses and Eleazar come down the mountain.
stops.quote: He said to him, 'Enter the cave', and he entered. He saw a bed already made and a light burning. He said to him, 'Ascend the bed', and he ascended. 'Stretch out your hands', and he stretched them out. 'Close your mouth', and he closed it. 'Close your eyes', and he closed them.
stops.quote_source: Rashi on Numbers 20:26, trans. M. Rosenbaum and A. M. Silbermann, via Sefaria
sources: Rashi on Numbers 20:26, citing Sifrei and Deuteronomy 32:50, via Sefaria
suggested_refs: Deuteronomy 10:6, which places Aaron's death at Moserah rather than Mount Hor, a contradiction the tradition never fully closes

stops.name: The camp below Mount Hor, thirty days of weeping
stops.date_confidence: Attested at Numbers 20:29, undated beyond following the death directly. The detail of the ministering angels showing the bier is Rashi's, from midrash.
stops.campa: Moses and Eleazar come down alone and the congregation sees that Aaron is dead. They do not believe it until the bier is shown to them. Then all the house of Israel weeps for him thirty days. Rashi marks the words: all the house, the women as well as the men, because Aaron pursued peace and made peace between a man and his fellow and between a man and his wife. For Moses, at the end of his own life, it will be the children of Israel who weep, which Rashi reads as the men. Not the same mourning.
stops.quote: all: both men and women, because Aaron used to pursue peace and promoted love between contending parties, and between man and wife
stops.quote_source: Rashi on Numbers 20:29, trans. M. Rosenbaum and A. M. Silbermann, via Sefaria
sources: Rashi on Deuteronomy 34:8, citing Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 17, via Sefaria
suggested_refs: Rashi on Deuteronomy 34:8, where the comparison between the two mournings is actually made

stops.name: Jerusalem, be of the disciples of Aaron
stops.date_confidence: The saying is attributed to Hillel the Elder, teaching in Jerusalem in the generation before the destruction of the Temple; no date attaches to its utterance. It is preserved in the Mishnah, compiled around 200 CE. The year here is a placement within Hillel's floruit.
stops.campa: Twelve centuries after Mount Hor, a teacher in Jerusalem gives his students a model to follow, and it is not Moses. Be of the disciples of Aaron, Hillel says: loving peace and pursuing peace, loving people and bringing them close to the Torah. The man remembered here is not the one who carried the rod into Pharaoh's court or wore the breastplate of judgment. It is the one the whole house of Israel wept for, women and men alike, because he made peace between a man and his wife.
stops.quote: Be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace, loving people and bringing them close to the Torah.
suggested_refs: Pirkei Avot 1:12, the saying of Hillel the Elder

stops.name: Jabal Harun, the monks on the summit
stops.date_confidence: The Finnish Jabal Harun Project excavated a Byzantine monastery and pilgrimage complex on the mountain between 1997 and 2013, with occupation running from about the fifth to the ninth century. The excavation reports were not obtained directly for this file; the account here rests on summary and is marked as reconstruction.
stops.campa: On the mountain above Petra, Christian monks build a monastery, a chapel, a hostel for pilgrims, and cisterns to hold what little water the rock will give. They build them around a spot already venerated as the grave of the high priest of Israel, and they keep the place for some four centuries. The pilgrims who climb to it are walking up the same slope the congregation watched three men climb, and only two come down. The mountain has been the tomb of Aaron for longer than it was ever anything else.
sources: Finnish Jabal Harun Project, University of Helsinki, excavation reports 1997-2013 (known through summary only)
suggested_refs: The Byzantine monastery and pilgrim hostel on the slope of Jabal Harun

stops.name: Canterbury, Aaron in the glass
stops.date_confidence: The typological glass cycle at Canterbury Cathedral was made in stages between about 1178 and 1220; the date given is a midpoint. The Biblia Pauperum block-book tradition that shares the same typological scheme is a later, fifteenth-century genre.
stops.campa: Glaziers set the high priest of Israel into a window at Canterbury, vested in mitre and jeweled breastplate, among the figures of the older covenant read as forerunners of the newer. In the block-books that spread the same scheme across Europe, Aaron stands paired with Christ as priest, his vestments the argument. The church that reads him this way has no interest in the calf or in the rod that swallowed the rods of Egypt. It wants only the garments, and the man who was told to put them on.
sources: Typological glass cycle, Canterbury Cathedral, c. 1178-1220
suggested_refs: The typological windows of Canterbury Cathedral and the Biblia Pauperum

stops.name: Mount Hor, the Latin pilgrim's account
stops.date_confidence: Burchard of Mount Sion wrote his Descriptio Terrae Sanctae around 1280. The text was not consulted directly for this file and the description of the Mount Hor shrine is known here at second hand only.
stops.campa: A Dominican friar from the Rhineland, travelling the Holy Land and writing down what he sees, records a shrine on Mount Hor kept as the tomb of Aaron. He is a Latin Christian describing a site that Jews revere as the grave of the first high priest and Muslims revere as the grave of the prophet Harun, and he climbs it as a pilgrim like the rest. No one holds the mountain. The friar goes up as one more visitor to a grave that three communities claim and none of them controls.
sources: Burchard of Mount Sion, Descriptio Terrae Sanctae, c. 1280 (known through summary only)
suggested_refs: Burchard of Mount Sion's Descriptio Terrae Sanctae, one of the fullest medieval Latin surveys of the Holy Land

stops.name: Jabal Harun, the white dome
stops.date_confidence: The inscription above the door gives 719 AH, which is 1319 or 1320 CE, in the reign of the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun. The pool material dated the building to 1458-1459 under Sultan Sayf al-Din Inal; no source supporting that could be reached, and it is withdrawn here.
stops.campa: At thirteen hundred and fifty metres, on the summit above Petra, the Mamluks raise a small sandstone building, ten metres by eight, with a courtyard and a single white dome that can be seen from the whole valley. The date of its renewal is cut above the door. Inside and around it, Mamluk dedications share the stone with Hebrew and Greek graffiti scratched by pilgrims. The tomb of Harun is a place where three scripts wait on one wall, over a grave that no excavation has ever tested and no one has ever asked to.
sources: Mamluk dedicatory inscription, 719 AH, above the shrine door
suggested_refs: The white-domed shrine of Nebi Harun on the summit of Jabal Harun

stops.name: London, Poussin's dance around the calf
stops.date_confidence: The Adoration of the Golden Calf is dated to about 1633-1634 and hangs in the National Gallery, London. The single year given is the earlier bound of that range.
stops.campa: Nicolas Poussin paints the Israelites dancing in a ring around the golden calf on its pedestal, and puts Aaron among them in white, gesturing toward the idol, presenting it. In the distance, small, Moses comes down the mountain with the tablets raised to break. The painter has read Exodus 32 and not Rashi. He gives no stalling, no altar built slowly to buy time, no feast set for the morrow. He gives the moment the brother arrives and sees, and he puts Aaron at the centre of it in white.
sources: Nicolas Poussin, 'The Adoration of the Golden Calf', c. 1633-1634, National Gallery, London
suggested_refs: Poussin's Adoration of the Golden Calf in the National Gallery, London
